idiom_name: enum State/Event + pure reduce fn + tokio::sync::watch state stream
implementation_notes: Rust maps the roles onto enums and channels: enum Event and enum State (or a struct with an enum phase) as closed types, fn reduce(&State, Event) -> State as the handler table, an mpsc channel feeding a single task that owns the state - sequential processing for free - and tokio::sync::watch as the state stream, documented as a channel that only retains the last sent value, whose Sender::subscribe() hands each new subscriber a Receiver at the current value (replay-one) and whose Receiver::changed() wakes on updates. futures::Stream is the general asynchronous-sequence abstraction when the state pipeline must be composed with other streams; without tokio the same design is built on futures::channel::mpsc plus a shared version counter.
pitfalls: watch keeps only the newest value: intermediate states are lost for slow subscribers, so use mpsc or broadcast when every transition must be observed for logging or analytics.
borrow() without borrow_and_update() can process the same value twice in a changed().await loop - the documented race those two methods exist to avoid.
The reducer task must be the single writer: sharing Arc<Mutex<State>> across tasks reintroduces uncoordinated mutation and re-entrancy.
watch::Sender::send fails once every Receiver is dropped; ignoring the error hides that the UI stopped listening and the state has no consumer.
